utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Wu Yi, who is from China and studied at the Korea University.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Kalbarczyk. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: [In English] Janusz Kalbarczyk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16th of June, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I intend to lead you on a couple of background details. You are a retired career military officer in the Polish Air Force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You retired with the rank of colonel after 25 years of service?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It's been 30 years of service, because the period of my studies is included in the period of service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In what year did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In April 1995, you were seconded from the Polish Air Force to the UN to serve in Bosnia as a military observer for one year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in the UN contingent, you held the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, 1995, you were deployed to Sector Sarajevo in the SE-1 Team in Pale, which was on the Bosnian Serb side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, I came to the mission in Zagreb. I was in Sarajevo about a week later, after training.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of training did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: So I learnt about the area of the sector. I also had refresher training in first aid, principles of patrolling, rules and regulations, anything that was related to UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe your duty as an UNMO, a United Nations Military Observer?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as a member of the team to which I was seconded, my duty was to strictly observe the rules and regulations, the rules and regulations governing UNMOs, take part in patrols, be on duty. Well, it's called to be on the radio duty. I was also asked to follow all the recommendations that were assigned to the sector, to the line. I was also responsible for reporting any cases which were important cases or significant cases that were incompatible with the regulations, and be also objective in whatever I was supposed to be doing. So that's, in a nutshell, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you also observing incoming and outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, during the fire, I never had an opportunity to observe, but I visited places which were subject or targets of firing, from which firing could have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And which places were these?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I specifically remember a place which is located over Sarajevo, where cannons were positioned, mortars, howitzers. And from these positions you could see Sarajevo very clearly, so I was surprised that it was so easy to fire shells at the town, if there was any shelling of the town from those positions. I cannot attest to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to your duty as an UNMO, were you or any member of your team armed with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, never. None of our team members had any guns, and I haven't seen anybody -- any other UNMO wearing any guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to events which began on the 26th of May, 1995. How many of the team were on duty that day?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: There were -- wait a minute, let me think. I think there were five of us. It was me, Evans, Kozusnik, Dmitri, and Pepe, who was a Spaniard, so five persons. And our team leader was on a leave of absence at the time. I came back a day earlier from my leave of absence. So on the 25th, there were five or six of us, and I mentioned them by their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, occurred mid-morning on the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, it so happened that I was on the radio duty. The weather was nice. I got up at about 7.00, 8.00 a.m., washed, and then reported readiness for duty to my headquarters in Sarajevo. I was only asked whether everything was okay, and I reported, yes, everything was okay. There was quiet around. At between 8.00 and 9.00, sirens blew in Pale. I was disoriented, I didn't know what was going on, but I saw people running away in the streets, trying to hide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anything subsequently occur around mid-morning?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. There was silence, quiet, afterwards. Then later, for about a half an hour, I heard the roar of a plane and, shortly afterwards, an explosion south-east of Pale. I saw smoke and air blast, strong air blast, which shattered, which reached our accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After that, did anyone come to your building?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: After this event, after this explosion, about half an hour later or 40 minutes later -- for about half an hour or 40 minutes later, there was -- nothing was happening in the building. I reported the explosion to my sector in Sarajevo. We got info to stay indoors, where we were stationed, not to leave the building, and to report any subsequent event. After about 40 minutes, a car came to our building. There were policemen -- three policemen in that car. They entered our building. The officer in command, in command of that team, had a pistol in his hand, uncocked. He pointed it at us, and the remaining other policemen had their Kalashnikov rifles, and they ordered us -- the officer actually ordered us to put our hands up. He informed us that we were arrested, and he also threatened us that if there was any other air-strike, we would be shot dead. After 10 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can -- if I could get you to pause there. When he said that you would be -- if there were any more air-strikes, you would be shot dead, was this coming from him or was this coming from someone else? Was he -- what did he actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, precisely, he said that he had an order to shoot us still.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone else come to the building that morning?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: After 10 minutes, the officer left the building. Only two policemen stayed, and they let us put our hands down. My interpreters started negotiating with these policemen. They wanted us to have some coffee. They wanted to ease the tension. And so it happened, everybody got coffee or tea to their liking. And after around 40 minutes, two cars pulled up outside the house. BSA soldiers got off the cars. There was a young officer in command, maybe 32, 33 years old, and they entered the building. The policemen and the soldiers started talking, the officer in command started talking to the policemen, and from what I could gather was that the policemen tried to explain to the officer that we were -- we had been under their control. The officer, in a very decisive tone, said that from then on, he was in charge, that we -- he said exactly that, from that very moment, we were being taken hostage by the army, by the BAS [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. When you said -- it was interpreted as "BAS" and earlier you said "BSA," what does this acronym stand for?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: They called themselves Bosnian Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So at that point when the military and the police had the discussion, did you then stay in the building? And if not, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: This was all in our presence. The discussion took place where we were, in the very same room. The soldiers that were accompanying the officer, they helped themselves to our belongings. They took our knives, pens, nothing that mattered, really. After all these explanations and exchanges, we got two minutes to take some of our belongings. He pointed out that we should take some warm clothes. And after that, we were taken outside, and we were chained, handcuffed in pairs. I was handcuffed with Zlatko Kozusnik, and we were taken to cars. Before that, the officer told us to give up our keys to the UN cars. In the car, I was handcuffed to my seat together with Kozusnik. There was a driver, military driver, in the front of the car. There was also another soldier with a Kalashnikov, and all the others were in other cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "all the others," are you talking about Evans and the person that you referred to as Pepe earlier?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the name of -- the surname of Pepe from Spain?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't recall. Generally, we addressed one another by first names, just like in our native tongues. I think it was Romero. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you were both -- put in two different vehicles, the team, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: We were put in four vehicles. Two cars were the cars that were used by the military that came to us, and the two cars were confiscated -- the UN cars were confiscated. I'm not sure how the others were distributed in the other cars, but there were four vehicles. They had four vehicles at their disposal. So in the car that I was in, there was just myself and Kozusnik. Now, from the building we went to the center of Pale. Then every vehicle stopped in the center. The doors were open, soldiers left the cars, and we were in some kind of market-place. There were quite a lot of civilians there, some soldiers as well. Some were very, very excited. They were excited with the victory, in inverted commas. So this is what I felt. They were overjoyed, they were laughing, they were mocking us, they insulted us, abused us verbally, and one of the civilians even came up to me and spat at my face. It was a very dangerous moment. This aggression that we witnessed, not everybody was involved, but this aggression grew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Pale for?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: We were there for about 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Then we could clearly see that they probably -- this is what I feel, that they got an order to leave fast and go to a place that I'm going to mention in a minute. We moved in the direction of a big explosion. As I learned later, we went to the very exact place where some ammunition depots were hit in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say you moved in the direction of a big explosion, was that in the direction of the explosion that you saw earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, so in the direction of the big explosion, and that was the very explosion. When we were nearing the place, I saw my colleagues who probably came earlier. It was like a valley, canyon, where some ammunition depots were masked or hidden. What was inside, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know -- did this area have a name?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I think it was generally called Jahorinski Potok, Jahorinski Potok or Canyon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw some colleagues. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a Russian UNMO; Patrick, from Lima 7 team. Both of them were there; and also a Czech, Olek [phoen], from Lima 7 as well. He was chained to the door of a storage facility, steel door. We were driving on into the canyon, and first Kozusnik had to get out of the car. He was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could just pause you there for a moment. Just going back to -- you mentioned the person called Patrick, and I know that you said you referred to people by their first names, but do you recall his second name at all?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Rechner, a Canadian UNMO. Rechner, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know the Czech UNMO that you are referring to as Olek? Do you know what his first or last name are?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, all of us called him "Olek," but I cannot recall his last name at this point. Well, we lived by the rule that we have no interest in each other's last names. Everyone was recognised based on our abbreviated names, but only in the documentation they would have our real names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could -- I would like you to watch a short video-clip now. It's 65 ter 40202A. If we could play the clip from 30:52 to 32:46.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, if you could watch the video on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a Russian from Lima 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we paused the tape at 31:06. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's Patrick, Patrick Rechner. He's Canadian. He's from Lima 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we paused the tape at 31:40. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, that's Patrick. This is Olek from Czech Republic. He was handcuffed to the warehouse door, and you can see his plaque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "his plaque," do you mean his patch on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, on his pant, a patch. But I can recognise his face very clearly. It was a young guy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We've stopped the tape at 32:02. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, more or less, that was the way we actually moved deeper into the canyon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. So you saw the Russian and Mr. Rechner handcuffed to the poles, and you also saw the Czech UNMO, Olek, who was handcuffed to the door of the ammunition depot. Did you and Kozusnik stay with these three UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I tender that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be admitted and given the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2153.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder -- I wonder whether the Trial Chamber has the interpretation of the journalist's words. Namely, the journalist says that they are suspected of having guided NATO aircraft towards Serbian targets. So it would be good if the Trial Chamber had the interpretation of the words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this video footage will be played with the witness who's testifying next Tuesday, who will -- and the transcript will be used with that witness. This witness simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the purpose of this witness, you wanted to identify the UNMOs who were in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He was clearly being driven by in a car and didn't hear what was being said on the video. He saw the images and saw the three men, so that was why I didn't use the transcript with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, I asked you whether you stayed with the three UNMOs that we just saw on the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Our vehicle passed these three UNMOs, and we were driving on into the canyon. After 200 metres, Kozusnik had to get out of the car, and he was handcuffed to some warehouse or to some pole - I don't remember correctly - and they were driving me further on in the direction of this big explosion. The place where I was handcuffed was the last building that remained in the proximity of the huge hole that remained after the explosion. There were also single minor explosions of the ammunition, or from time to time we could hear the explosions. I was handcuffed to the lightning road [as interpreted]. The soldiers were doing this very quickly, rather quickly. I could guess they were in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could just pause there, Mr. Kalbarczyk. The interpretation said you were handcuffed to the lightning road. You meant "lightning rod" or you said "lightning rod," did you not?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It was kind of a line that leads a current to the ground, the current.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were single minor explosions of the ammunition from time to time. Was that during the time that you were handcuffed to this lightning rod?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this was this place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How close were these explosions to where you were handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: About 60, 80 metres. So this was a threat to me, but at the time I was not thinking about it that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For what purpose did you think that you were being handcuffed to this installation?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, I could have guessed easily that the Serbs were expecting another air-strike and we served as human shields, protecting these locations or these facilities which were of strategic importance for them. This is how I understood that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long were you handcuffed to this rod?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: About four and a half hours. It was in scorching sun. After about two hours, two soldiers brought me a piece of bread and a can, but without any can opener. I hadn't got any water, either, and I needed water most. Ten metres away from me, there was a brook, a somewhat small stream, with pure water. They gave me the food, and they were in a hurry to leave this place as quickly as possible. And after another two, two and a half hours, so altogether it was four and a half hours I was there, the two soldiers came in a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just get you to pause there. When you were first taken to the rod, were you videotaped? Was footage taken of you at the rod?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when I was being chained, handcuffed, an officer with a film camera came, and he was filming me being chained to that place, to the rod, in the place where I was brought to, and he didn't say a word.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were there for four to four and a half hours. Can you just describe for the Trial Chamber what you were going through during this period?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was very stressed. I was prepared to die. I thought that these air-strikes could be repeated and there is a real possibility of me being killed during the air-strike, repeated air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So then you mentioned that after, two soldiers came in a car?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you leave the -- did you leave the depot where you were?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. They unchained me. They took me -- put me in the vehicle. And on our return journey, they also took or picked Rechner, in other words, Patrick. As regards the other colleagues, they were left in the places in which they were chained. We drove in the direction of Pale, and we got to the check-point as you leave Pale in the direction of Sarajevo. The car stopped there, and we were blindfolded. In the car, there was the driver. He was a military driver. There was a cameraman, a civilian. I guess he was a journalist, some journalist. And there was another soldier, masked, with a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could ask you to now watch a short video-clip. It's 65 ter 40557C.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just pause there. Sorry, we paused at .21 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise anything in that short piece of footage we just saw?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I recognise myself. I can't see -- I can't tell you who is on the side, sitting on the side, but I guess it's Patrick.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what are you wearing?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I'm wearing a summer uniform. This was the uniform -- I was on duty when I was first arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what colour is the uniform?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It's blue, blue shirt, blue trousers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could stop the video there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, were you told where you were being taken before you were blindfolded or before you were both blindfolded?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: From the moment we were unchained in the first location I mentioned, nobody has ever told us anything, where we're going, what we're going there for. Everything was happening without any words spoken. When I was being blindfolded, I was not told why this was being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how were you feeling at this point as you were driving along up the road?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I felt that the worst could happen, that we were being taken to a location where we would be shot down which they were intending to film. Patrick was also very upset, and I could sense that looking at him. The road we were driven along was bumpy. It was a road in the mountains. The vehicle was jumping up and down. It was kind of a road in the mountains, full of stones and an uneven surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said that you -- Patrick was also very upset, you could sense that by looking at him, clearly, that was when you were back before the blindfolds were on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's right, that's correct. I could see then that neither him nor me realised where we would be taken. And when we were blindfolded, our fears grew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When the blindfolds were taken off, did you know where you were? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I didn't know where I was. I knew that I was at the top of some mountain. There were remains of snow there. I saw a big antenna, spherical in shape. And I was very thirsty. I asked to get some water, which I got. When I drank that water or when I was drinking that water, a civilian journalist approached me and told me not to worry, that nothing wrong was going to happen to us here, that we're going to be filmed only. This was the turning point -- breakthrough point in this course of our anxiety, and I believed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, if I could just halt you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender the last video footage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that they said that -- the journalist said that he was going to film you. Did anything happen between then, that point, and when you were actually filmed?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. I knew all of this, and I had my bag with me that I took from my POB, and therefore I decided to change into my field uniform, one that you can expect on such trips. I put it on the blue uniform. Therefore, in the pictures, in the footage, you can see that I'm wearing my field uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Once you'd changed into your uniform, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When I changed, I was taken to the antennas and situated on some kind of concrete base. They chained me to something. Behind my back, I had a soldier with a gun. I did not consent to any interview. The journalist asked me to say briefly -- to tell him briefly what had happened, and this is what I did. I believed that this was the moment when I could tell the headquarters how we were and what our situation was. From the very moment we were detained, we didn't have any contact with our sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could ask you to watch a short video-clip. It's 65 ter 40202B. And if we can play from .37:23 to .38:14, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just thinking. With the translation, if we could actually play it again, and if the interpreters could translate into English. And for the benefit of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give it a try?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, did you recognise what was in that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. This is the very first moment. You can see my hand being down. I'm handcuffed or chained to something, to some kind of maybe rod, pole, some kind of steel pipe maybe. While I was sitting there chained, I was watching what was happening downhill, and I saw Patrick standing close to a car. And I saw two colleagues, UNMOs, 50 metres from me, maybe, on my left-hand side, and they were sitting on the grass with their backs turned to each other. They were handcuffed, their hands were handcuffed. One of them was white-skinned and one -- and the other one was dark-skinned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of either of those two UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall the name of the African guy, but one of the white-skinned people was -- I think he was Czech. I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think he was from Czechoslovakia, says the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If we could play the video again, and with the benefit of the translation into English of what's being said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "UNPROFOR members have also been positioned to other strategically important facilities that might be targets of NATO air-strikes." "Of course." "Why?" "I don't know what you're doing for me." "Are you afraid of NATO air-strikes?" "I am afraid, because I don't know when they might come." "The international community and its decisions have brought the situation upon these people. Whether they are going to survive depends on NATO actions."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, how long did you stay handcuffed to this radio antenna -- radar antenna? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Just for the filming, around 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, what did you understand the purpose of being handcuffed to this installation?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I think it's easy to guess. The Serbs wanted to show the world, to the NATO command, that any further air-strikes might result in a tragedy for us. It was hinted that we were human shields in various strategic targets that they wished to protect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So after the 15 minutes or so that you were there, where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In the same team, we went -- we went into the cars. We drove down. We stopped outside a building that looked modern. It fit well within the -- in the landscape. It looked like some remnant maybe from the Olympics. And there, we were invited to a meal. We were given some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you -- where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In that place that I mentioned just a minute ago -- in that place, we were just an hour, maybe 90 minutes, and then we returned to Pale, to the base, where there was a barracks building, two-floor building, and that was our accommodation for the night. Everything ended by 8.00 p.m. I met all my colleagues that I saw, and I met colleagues that I have not seen earlier. There were 11 of us in the barracks at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you spoken to by a military officer that evening about what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Approximately at 9.00 p.m., after one hour upon arrival, after we talked amongst each other, there was an officer coming. He was a major. He looked quite serious. He was 50 or 55 years old. He made a good impression upon us. He was very calm and very to the point. He said that there are no threats at night, but this is all that he may tell us. He cannot tell us what's going to happen on the next day. He said that he may assure us that we shall have a quiet sleep at night. And we liked that, because we were really looking and we missed even tough but very concrete and substantial information on what's going to happen. We had a lot of questions to this officer, but he had one answer for us, I do not know what may happen later. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he mention anything in relation to what would happen to you if the air-strikes continued?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that our status is not going to change as long as the parties fail to reach an agreement. In other words, there must be a clear declaration from the NATO command that they will stop air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or what would happen to you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Tactics were very transparent to us. Serbs wanted to have us the closest to the sites that were important to them. They wanted to have the capability to chain us to the strategic targets at the very short time, and that's what happened. On the next day, we woke up. We were able to wash. We had breakfast, and we were carried to the place -- to the new place that we have never seen before. And to reach that place, we were driving along the narrow asphalt road. At some point, there was a barrier, and there was like a barrack on the side, and they had the room where they could easily accommodate 11 of us. In that room, they detained us. Our understanding was that as soon as they get a signal from the Serb command headquarters, from that place they would take us to unknown locations. It never happened, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that was your understanding, but was anything actually said to you in that respect in those terms?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. At this new place, no one informed us what is the purpose of our -- of us staying there. That was our guessing, based on what we heard from the officer the night before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how long were you kept in this building for?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, here I have a memory gap, but it seems to me that we probably spent one night in that building because I remember that upon the return -- I do not remember spending the second night in the same barrack building where we spent the first night, so most likely we stayed overnight in that place and the day after we were transferred to another building, where we spent the rest of the time until we were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that other -- sorry. If I can interrupt you. That other building that you were subsequently moved to, where you stayed until you were released, was that back at the military barracks, where you were taken originally, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the building in the same base where the other barracks was located, but this building was closer to the gate and it was of the smaller size. But the building that I'm talking about right now was not within the parameter of the base, it was beyond the base, and most likely we spent the whole day and night over there. We were there overnight, because we had our personal belongings with us, so we were able to spend the night there. We didn't have a bed or anything. I think that we were just laying down on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, during the day, and this is the 27th of May, 1995, we're talking about now, you mentioned earlier that you probably spent one night in that building, because when you returned -- where -- and then you paused. Where were you taken on the 27th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: 27th of May, as I said earlier, well, the whole day we spent in that building. But what happened there? To me, an important development was that it was the second time when the same Serbs came with a car. And they took me and the Brazilian, Harley, and we were driven back to the same place where I was filmed next to the radar antenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just describe briefly for the Trial Chamber what happened when you were taken with Harley to the radar station?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When we were taken there, I didn't know where we were going. But since I was familiar of the road when you're leaving Pale in the direction of Sarajevo, that was the road when we were stopped at the Serbian check-point, and again we were being blindfolded, I guessed we were going in the same direction. I was then much more calm. I tried to be calm for the sake of Harley, to calm him down, to show to him that he should not be nervous. I was educating to him that we were probably being taken to the place to be filmed again. And that's what -- that was the case. We came to the same place, and I was again chained to the antenna. Harley was chained to some other part on that peak, and we were both filmed. I used this opportunity and I answered the question put by the journalist about my feelings. Knowing that I would be watched by my family, I simply said that I was okay, I had food, I had shelter for the night. That was my intention, so that in this way I could pass on some information for them to calm down. I knew my wife -- I knew that she trusted my words, what I'm saying. And although I knew that my words were very short, there was some meaning, substance, content in them. That's it. And another thing. After we've been filmed - that took about 15 to -- 10 to 15 minutes, or maybe 20 minutes - we were brought back by the same road to join our colleagues -- where we joined our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll pause you there. I'd like you to watch a short video-clip now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 40202D. And if we could play it from 40:35 to 43:21, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we -- sorry, if we just could pause there. If I could -- if the interpreters could interpret what's being said into English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Members of United Nations forces are still at the locations where they were put by the Serbian army. They accompanied by guards and they have no problems, as they will confirm themselves. At the same time, NATO aeroplanes are still circling Serbian skies, threatening to unload their deadly cargo. Of course, it remains to be seen whether they will actually do so. It is now upon the international community to show everything it can do, because so far the only thing they showed is that they can bomb the innocent Serbian population." The interpreter can no longer follow because the text has been scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could continue -- sorry. If you could -- we're pausing at 41:18.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, you recognise the person that's in that shot?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's the Brazilian UNMO whom we called "Harley," just used that name to call him on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can continue playing the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we play back from 41:15, for example, so that the interpreters could follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... threatening to unload their deadly cargo. Of course, it remains to be seen whether they will actually do so. It is now upon the international community to show everything it can do, because so far the only thing they showed is that they could bomb the innocent Serbian population and --" Again, the text is scrolled up too fast. Interpreter's note: We need to have the transcript in writing in order to be able to follow properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We could have paused it when the interpreters stopped interpreting, and then we can continue. I will ask the interpreters when to start again. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... whether it will actually be done remains to be seen. It is now upon the international community to show everything it can do, because so far the only thing they showed is that they can bomb the innocent Serbian population. And now let us see if they will bomb members of units they are sending to our land as well." "Captain Harley --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can continue now. We have interpreted it all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Captain Harley, are you still afraid today?" "Of course, I fear for all of us." "What are you afraid of?" "I'm anxious. We are in a bad position. This situation we're in is bad, and we are very sorry because of that." "Do you have a message for your people, for NATO pilots?" "I try to trust the good sense of politicians and people that are in charge and who decide about our future. Let them stop this. This is a stupid war." "Do you have any problems with Serbian soldiers?" "No. Serbian soldiers and their commanders behave very well, as true professionals." "I didn't have any problems --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We've paused at 42:46, and we've just seen the end of Harley's interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What do you see on the screen now, Mr. Kalbarczyk?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I can see myself in my gala uniform, in my dress uniform. And, what I said before, my short statement given to the journalist. I'm giving my opinion about the behaviour of the Serbian Army towards us, and I think it was a positive behaviour towards us, and I'm passing on information for my family to calm down, not to worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. We will listen to what you have to say. If we can continue -- I'm sorry. If we can continue, we will actually hear what you had to say to the reporter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I want to say to my family that they shouldn't worry, that everything is okay." "Did you have enough food and drink?" "Yes, food and drink, and water to wash myself." "These are the words of United Nations members who are now located at the facilities of the Serbian Army. Their future depends on the future actions of NATO and the international community."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, that clip that we just watched, 65 ter 40202D, is, in fact, Exhibit P2143. We watched that on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So when we admitted Exhibit P2143, we did not admit the audio part, so we'll replace it with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, what do you see in the -- sorry. If we can just stop that there. We've finished that. Where were you and Harley then taken?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: You mean after we've been filmed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: We were driven down, back to the building in which we were on the first day. We were treated to a lunch. There was actually a wedding reception at that place of some Serbian family, and it turned out that one of the Serbian soldiers was the organiser of that wedding reception. He was an elderly man. He recognised me because we had met on one of the patrols when I visited his post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you eventually go back to the barracks? You were saying -- earlier, you were saying that you were unsure as to whether you went back to the other building which was outside the military barracks compound or you went, in fact, back to the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Nobody told us where we would be taken back, but intuitively I assumed that we would be rejoined with our colleagues. And we did come back to the place where our colleagues were from which we had been taken. It was not a return to the military base, but to that barracks where in the morning we were taken on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I think you said earlier in your testimony that you then moved back to a building -- a smaller building near the entrance to the military barracks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It's not really correct, because that happened on the 29th. And I remember that this was connected with the fact that there were too many of us, given the number of beds in that new building. In that new building, there were only eight beds, so to say, so there was enough room for eight persons. So it was suggested that the two Russian UNMOs would be transferred, and I was also asked whether I wanted to be transferred. And then I think it was Patrick who said to me that they were to be transferred to the Ukrainian Battalion. Whether this was true or not, I cannot confirm. I did not agree to be transferred. I said that I wanted to stay with my team, and that was the case. The Russians left, and one of us left as well. I don't remember who that was. So there were eight of us who stayed behind. On the 29th, we were transferred to a new place, a new location in the base at which we spent our first night after the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this was in the small building near the entrance to the barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it was a small building maybe 50 metres from the main gate. I think -- from a soldier's point of view, I think it might have been a building for those guarding the gate. There were two places to sleep in, there was a bathroom, shower, and there was a larger room, like a living-room, with a TV set.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see out of the building?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. Out of our windows, we could see some of the base. You could see the traffic through the entry gate, vehicles coming in, out. We could saw people -- we could see people coming in and out. We could see that from our windows. For one week, we were restricted, we were banned from leaving the building. What did I see? I saw a lot of movement of military vehicles. Especially towards the evening, I could see trucks leaving with soldiers, and I assumed that they were going to do night duty. And then in the morning, they came back. I saw vehicles coming with some command officers or from command posts. It was also said -- rumoured that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic and other commanders came there, but, personally, I didn't see Dr. Karadzic there in the base.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic in the base?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, just one time. I think after two, three days, when we were accommodated in the new building, a few people in civilian clothes came to us. They were wearing civilian clothes, and they checked on us, they checked the accommodation. Later, when we were able to watch TV, when we were allowed to watch TV, I actually recognised that one of the civilians had been General Mladic. When we were able to watch TV, I could see him in his uniform, and I could actually see that this was the very same person I had seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit P00653, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, do you see the photograph that's on the screen? Do you recognise anyone in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. In the foreground, I recognise General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's the person -- is that the person that you say you saw in civilian clothes in the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The first time when I saw him in our barracks, he was wearing civilian clothes. And while I actually make this association, this link, I saw him in uniform on TV, and I'm not sure whether, on TV, he was wearing the very -- this very same uniform, but I remember his face, characteristic features, and I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did Mladic stay in the barracks on the -- at the time that you saw him during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: His visit lasted around 30 minutes. During that visit, my colleagues, Evans, a Ghanian UNMO, and Olek from Lima 7, a Czech UNMO, were invited to talk. I didn't take part in this conversation. Right after we left the barracks, I learned that they had been asked whether they were able, physically, to guide NATO planes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who was asking them these questions?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I didn't take part in this conversation. I was also told that -- they told me that they had been asked about myself, whether I -- whether they had any knowledge about my skills or abilities when it comes to guiding planes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you're talking about "they," do you mean Evans and Olek?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that's who I mean, Evans and Olek. This was when I -- when the civilian-clad people went away. They came back, and obviously we talked to one another. We were also being filmed by a cameraman. We were unshaved, we had beards, because we were -- we had been forbidden to shave. There was no interview, we had not been interviewed, and we also noticed at that time that Mr. Karadzic was not filmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness corrects himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did any of the UNMOs require any medical assistance? And if so, were you able to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The Spaniard, Pepe, was in the worst condition out of all of us. It was fortunate enough that two weeks after the 26th -- sorry, I have to correct myself. That was earlier. I think it was on the 3rd or 4th of June the representatives of the Red Cross came to us, two women, as far as I can remember, and we could ask for some essentials. For example, we lacked some basics like tooth-brushes, toothpaste, underwear. And we also said that we would like a doctor to see us. And that was when I also wrote a letter to my family, to my wife. And I asked the women that came to see us to send the letter to Poland, and they did send it. The letter reached Poland. Two days after the Red Cross women left, a doctor came to our building. We were examined. He talked to us, and he said -- he stated that my Spanish colleague is in a bad condition, is in bad health. He had some heart problems. The doctor wrote a decision that this colleague should be released. That was, indeed, the case. Pepe was the first UNMO who was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When were you told that you would be released?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The time until I was informed about the release was taking long. Meanwhile, other colleagues were released. I don't remember the actual sequence, but I was informed on the 13th of June, in the morning. I was informed by Captain Vojvodic. He was our liaison officer. I packed my things, and I was transferred to Pale. It was a police station in Pale. And on the second time, I actually met the same officer that detained us on Day 1. At that place, we were waiting for the buses to arrive, and the buses took us to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could just pause you there. You said from the police station?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you actually taken somewhere else before you were put on the buses?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Next to the police station, there was a container. And once they checked my personal details, that was where they locked me. Actually, there were many other people there who were transferred there earlier than myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just stop there for the moment. Your Honour, it's time for the break. I have a couple of documents and a couple of short video-clips that I wish to show the witness after the break, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break, then. We'll break for half an hour and resume at three minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could introduce Chelsea Sayles, who is a lawyer from the United States working with us today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, before the break you said that you were taken from the police station and then locked into a container. What happened after you came out of the container? Or, first of all, how long were you kept in the container?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was just one container, and we spent three to four hours in that place. It was very stuffy there. There was no window, and there were quite many people inside. After four hours, we were allowed to leave the container. They asked us to stand in double file, and at that point I noticed that we were surrounded by the soldiers wearing red berets, and they were supposed to escort us to Novi Sad. They were reading the list of names, and we followed the list and we were getting on the bus. When they finished reading, the convoy was formed and we took off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If I could ask for 65 ter 11722 to be brought up on the screen. This is a document -- an order dated the 13th of June, 1995, from Mr. Karadzic regarding the captured UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it states there: "At 11.00 a.m. on the 13th of June, 1995, release all captured UN soldiers and inform them that they are free to go or continue performing their duties from before the incident which led to their capture." "2. Hand over to Mr. Jovica Stanisic all the captured UNPROFOR soldiers and military observers, including all French, all British, two Polish and two other soldiers, except 15 military observers who will remain in our custody at Pale until Sunday, 13th of June, 1995. Return the personal effects and weapons to all released UNPROFOR soldiers and military observers." First of all, is this order consistent with your experiences? Were two Polish officers released on that day?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. In the container, I met my colleague, a Pole, Major Wojtasiak, and there was another person who joined us, Zlatko. As far as other UNMOs are concerned, other UNMOs who were with me at the base, I had no knowledge what is going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Zlatko you referred to was Kozusnik from the Czech Republic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's correct, Zlatko Kozusnik from the Czech Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2156.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could ask you to now watch a short video-clip. It's 65 ter 40202C, and if we can play it from 2:11.13 to 2.13:08.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could pause there at 2.11.31.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that there were people with red berets who were to escort you to Serbia, to Novi Sad. Do you see, on the screen at the moment, a soldier with a red beret in front of the bus?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this what you were referring to when you said "a soldier with a red beret"?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I can see only one. There were many more, about 20. So we were about 20 on the bus, so there were many more soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could continue with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could pause there, please, at 2:11:42.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's shown in that shot?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it's me on the bus. So that means my name must have been called out, because I'm on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... 18 days. We were treated correctly throughout the entire time. And now we're in the hands of the federal security service. No complaints."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could stop the video there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the last person? Did you recognise not this person on the screen right now, but the one just before in the glasses? Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, because later I served together with him on the team in Dubrovnik. He's a Swedish UNMO, Gunnar, Gunnar. That's the name, Westlund, Gunnar Westlund.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I tender that video-clip, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I hope that the Trial Chamber has been provided with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The translation was actually read by the interpreters, what was said by Mr. Westlund on that clip, Mr. Karadzic. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I remember having heard the sound, but I take it -- it's not noted in the transcript, but I don't think we heard many. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the transcript is also in e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could watch another short video-clip. This is 65 ter 40387B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We have here with us 26 members of the French-British battalion and 2 members of the Polish battalion, a Swede, a Russian, a Czech, and a Norwegian. "Sixteen French, six English, two Polish --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They will be handed over, just like the last time, to their headquarters in Belgrade. There are 15 men remaining, and we hope that during the coming two, three days, we will take them over. As has already been said, due to technical reasons, we have not been able to take them over yet. We are happy that the entire mission has been completed successfully. We have already stated that in terms of political and security reasons, it was a very complex mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person that was being interviewed in that video?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that man and I don't recall this statement, because when we were being taken, all that was done was this list was read out. And based on that, we were boarding the bus. And I don't recall these photographs I see now and these people in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, again, is what he said consistent with what happened that day, that there were two Poles in the list of people that were being released that day?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I understood, the interpretation understood, that there were two Polish members of a battalion. I was not a member of a Polish battalion. I was not a member of a mission. I was just a member of the UNMOs, so I don't understand this statement made in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of us on the bus were observers, not members of battalions. Perhaps those who were mentioned here as members of the French Battalion were members of the French Battalion, but I was not a member of any battalion. I was only an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kalbarczyk. That will be Exhibit P2158.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, when you got to Novi Sad, where were you taken, where were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In Novi Sad, we were taken to a holiday resort. It looked like it was a holiday resort, and each one of us got his own room with a bathroom. We were treated to supper. We arrived there in the evening, and that was the end of the day. So when the bus came to Novi Sad, we were greeted -- actually, I was greeted by the Polish consul from Belgrade and a few people from Poland. They congratulated me on being there. And, basically, in Novi Sad, in this holiday resort which, ironically, was called "Sloboda," which is "Freedom," we felt released, although we still were under the custody of the Serbian Army. We didn't have complete freedom, we couldn't leave the perimeter of the holiday resort. That's it, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I just want to now show you a few documents and ask you whether certain aspects of these documents are consistent with your experiences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 18931, please. This is a document dated the 14th of June. It's a UN daily report to the Security Council from Akashi to Annan on the release of hostages and inability of UNHCR convoys for the enclaves to obtain clearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It states there that: "Twenty-six hostages (detained personnel) have been released and are currently in Novi Sad, waiting to be handed over to the Serbian authorities." It also says in the first paragraph that Dr. Karadzic announced that 15 hostages that would be released later due to technical reasons. Is this consistent with your experience, that some of your UNMO colleagues were not released and were back at the military barracks in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I was the first one on the 13th, in the morning at 10.00, who left this barrack. After about an hour, Kozusnik joined, and none other of my team joined us. So on that day, only two persons were released, me and Kozusnik. And later, I learnt, after I was released, that the others -- the other on our team were still detained by Serbs, but the circumstances did not allow me to follow the events and I don't know whether they were in that very same place or whether they were transferred to some other place, because after my release, I had a number of other different things to attend to and I didn't follow their fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's admitted as Exhibit P2159.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, on the 14th of June, 1995, where did you go from Novi Sad? Just very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: From Novi Sad, in the morning we were transported to the airport in Belgrade, where a plane was awaiting for us. The plane took us to Zagreb. And after I landed in Zagreb, we were free.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like 65 ter 21111 to be brought up. Your Honour, I seek leave to use this document and the next document. I have discussed -- both documents have been discussed with Mr. Robinson, who has no objection to them being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's granted. Please move on, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This document, 21111, is dated the 14th of June, 1995. It's an UNPROFOR code cable, hostages released on the 13th of June, 1995. In fact, it's from the special representative of the force commander in Belgrade. If we could go to -- the first paragraph says: "Please find enclosed the list of 26 released UN personnel coming from seven countries, including of eight UNMOs." Number 2: "They will probably formally be handed over at 12.00 noon on the 14th of June, 1995." If we could go to the third page, please. You looked at this document yesterday in preparation for your testimony. Do you see your name in the attached list?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, in item 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 21112. This is another document dated the 14th of June, again from the special representative of the force commander in Belgrade, hand-over of detained UNPF personnel on the 14th of June, 1995. It says, in paragraph 1, that the UN personnel have been treated well and that they are, of course, concerned about their remaining friends. If we could turn to the next page of the document, and paragraph 3 says: "I handed over our information about 15 hostages that are still not released as Annex B." And the next paragraph, that they will be released before the end of the week. And if we can go to the next page, and this lists the 15 persons -- UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we see there that there's nine UNMOs last seen in Pale on the 13th of June, 1995, by the UNMOs released on the 13th of June, 1995. Location believed to be at the BSA barracks located two kilometres south-east of Pale on the right-hand side of the road to Foca. And then there lists Captain Rechner, Captain Zidlik, Soldier Evans, Major Gelissen, Captain Alves, Captain Al Lawwama, Captain Laine, Commander Schan deler, and Lieutenant-Colonel Niagi. Do you -- when you said a moment ago that there was certain number of your colleagues left back at the barracks when you left Pale, were these the people you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I can see here the names of Rechner, that's Patrick; Zidlik, that's Olek; Evans. I don't know whether Captain Alves is Harley or not, that Brazilian guy. I don't know that. I would have to see his first name. All I can see is "Alves." I don't know the Brazilian by that name. I had no opportunity to learn his surname. So definitely the three persons at the top I mentioned, but when it comes to the others, the other names, I don't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the last document is a map, 65 ter 23077.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The map that will appear on the screen is a map that was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor using 65 ter 19082 as the base map, and overlaid onto this map are the different locations in Bosnia where you were held during your period of detention from the 26th of May to the 13th of June, 1995. You had an opportunity to review this map in preparation of your testimony, and you made an addition to be included on the map at the location of Jahorinski Potok, where you were taken on the 26th of May, 1995. Looking at the map in front of you, does that accurately reflect your movements during the period that you were held by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Graphically, this could be shown on the map this way, how I moved once or a couple of times, including the return to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's shown by the lines with the arrows? Your Honour -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. I do -- I understand the arrows, yeah, go forth and back, and, indeed, this is the -- this illustrates and reflects what I said here before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Kalbarczyk, can you tell the Court how -- how this ordeal during the 26th of May to the 1st of June, how that had an impact on you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It is hard, really, to describe it in words. I wouldn't wish such experience on anyone, the experience that I witnessed. That was my experience or my colleagues' -- experiences of my colleagues. Well, impact on my life? What's positive is that my life has changed. I started to value it more, and in everything I did after I left the military, I became more sensitive. I am a person more sensitive to human suffering. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions, and there are no associated exhibits to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Colonel Kalbarczyk. You will be cross-examined by Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kalbarczyk.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just briefly like to go over your statement. Let's remind ourselves how you saw those things in November 1995, when you first provided your statement. On page 2 -- or, rather, page 1 of your statement, you say that five days prior to the 26th, you had received certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Do we have a photocopy of his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I fully expected that the Prosecution has provided that to the witness. It must be in e-court. I don't know under what number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 90208, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your kindness, Ms. Sutherland. But it's for you to put it to that witness if you are minded to ask questions in relation to his statement. Let's bring it up on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 90208, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, we are told it hasn't been yet released. So it is being done by Mr. Reid, I noted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may take a moment, so Mr. Karadzic may wish to ask some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have a print-out, so why don't you -- why don't we put it on the ELMO so that all of us can follow. And in the meantime, why don't you put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, indeed, here is a hard copy of the document. Can we first look at the first page and then the following page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the third paragraph. On the 22nd of November, 1995, you provided this statement; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the third paragraph, where it says: [In English] "About five days before May the 26th ..." [Interpretation] At that time, your movement was restricted, you could not conduct patrols, and you had to stay in your accommodation. You were allowed to go shopping in Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's right, Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know already at that time that there would be NATO air-strikes, that NATO air-strikes were going to take place?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I didn't know, and our team leader didn't inform us about this. We were only restricted for movement. We were told that we can only go out to equip ourselves with some essentials only in the morning and early afternoon, and we couldn't go to all places. We were restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any information as to why the change had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Let me add here that in the statement it says that "about five days before the 26th of May." Within these five days, I was allowed to go on leave of absence. This was my first leave of absence. And it is hard for me to say whether there were any additional details, any additional information that was given to the team regarding our restricted movement. I returned from my leave on the 25th of May, i.e., one day before the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to let you know that the document has been released and we can see it through e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, we have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So five days prior to the 26th of May, you were on furlough, right, and you only heard that there had been restrictions on movement?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. I was on leave a maximum for three, four days, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that time, were you aware of the Muslim offensive which started on the 1st of May and then intensified after the 15th of May, and that Muslim offensive targeted Serbian positions around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I was focused on the tasks performed in my sector. Please note that I had been in the sector for less than three weeks. I was still learning what the terrain was, what the area was about. I had only been there for three weeks. I came to Zagreb on the 13th of April. I received training there. Then I was transported to Sarajevo, where I spent around three days and further trained, and only then was I directed to Pale. So in Pale, I was probably on the 20th of April; Pale, i.e., the place where I was UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to look at the middle of the last paragraph, where it says that: [In English] "... but the officer in charge told us that from now on, we were under the custody of the Vojska Republike Srpske (BSA). Nobody tried to mistreat us." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Earlier on today, you mentioned the same thing, and you told that you had been told that you were hostages. That was on page -- I can't see the page number. Can you quote those words exactly? Is it true that you were told that you were under the custody of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, these words were uttered with this meaning, with the meaning that they were taking over -- they were taking us over from the police officers. And the officer -- the military officer said -- and I'm not sure what he said exactly, I mean, how to say it. He said we were arrested by the military of the Serbian Republic, that they are taking us over from the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, he wasn't the one who used the word "hostages"?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, the word "hostage" was not used at that time. But in a moment, we actually learned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Thank you. Can we go to the next page of the same document, please. How did you perceive the attitude of the military, the police, and the civil population towards you during those three weeks? Did they show any hostile feelings towards you?
