And when I say "you," I don't mean you, personally, but all of you, you and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As for civilians, I can only tell you about the incident in the -- in central Pale, when we were being transported for the first time to the place where they wanted to handcuff us and treat us as human shields. Most civilians back then were very hostile. However, I'm not saying that everyone was. As for the army officers and the policemen, I would say that most of them were very correct in their behaviour. There were just very few people who demonstrated their reluctance towards us. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I may not have been very precise in my question. Before the air-strikes, did you have any impression that there were hostilities towards you? How were you received by the military and by the civilians before the air-strikes? Did anybody display any hostile feelings towards you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I think that it was similar to the situation after that. Overall, I kept a positive attitude in my memory. Both the military personnel, police officers, and civilians showed positive attitude. What I should say, that they were correct in their behaviour, but they were not friendly. When I was on my leave, I talked to my wife, and I used exactly the same words. I said that I feel well in Serbia, that there is no unfriendly attitude that I would feel there, the way they showed it on TV or the way they covered it in the press. And it was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, I see the transcript mentions "Serbia." I don't know that the witness said that or there's a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Colonel Kalbarczyk? Did you say that you felt well in Serbia, that there was no unfriendly attitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "Serbia," I meant the location where I was deployed, Pale area, and just that particular location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me assist you. You probably meant "Republika Srpska." Right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that republic existed at that point in time. There was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now could I draw your attention to the middle part of the second paragraph, where it says: [In English] "In my opinion, that stop in the main street of Pale was very dangerous for us because there are many soldiers and civilians around the car. The soldiers left the car with the door open, and we were threatened and insulted. One civilian spit on me -- at me." [Interpretation] When you were arrested, at one point you stopped in the center of Pale for some reason. The air-strikes had already started. You were recognised by some civilians and soldiers who were passing by. Did they recognise your uniform and your blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I'm not sure what they saw in us. I was describing the reaction of people who were gathered there. And today, I believe that it was a mistake made by our escorts, because that incident might have turned into a very unpleasant situation; hence, the example of spitting, when one of the civilians spat at me. They were allowed to approach us very close, people that I never knew, strangers, and they could actually hit us with their hands or they could harm us otherwise. Our escorts, after a while they realised that this situation is getting dangerous, and they closed the door and we departed. So that was my understanding of that incident at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The point I was making, Colonel, was this: They did not know you, personally. They never accused you of anything, personally. They just recognised your uniform and your helmet, and they realised that you were a UN member, and that was why they were hostile towards you; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps your reasoning is like that, but then you need to remember that we were walking around that town, we were shopping there. If these were the same people, it would be hard for them not to recognise us. And earlier, we felt that they were showing correct behaviour towards us. So where that aggressive behaviour was coming from at the moment when we found ourselves in such a predicament?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the questionnaire that you filled out after you were released, on page 3 you say that you had been told by the Serbs that they thought that the United Nations and NATO were one-and-the-same thing; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, many times we heard this objection raised against our UNMOs that us and NATO are -- is the same, but we are working together. They did not accept our arguments where we were trying to separate ourselves very clearly from that thinking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now can we look at the third page from here. The next one, please, 64. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the end of the second paragraph, where you say: [In English] "In that new accommodation, the atmosphere was better, and we had good relations with the BSA officers. We had hot water. I think that we could not go outside because they were afraid of possible provocations of BSA soldiers who were passing near our building. After about a week, we were allowed to go outside. I stayed there until my release." [Interpretation] Do you think that the Serbian officers were afraid of the provocations coming from the soldiers who were passing by and that's why they didn't allow you to go out? When you say "they were afraid," who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: What I meant, those that were in charge. We were under their custody. As an officer, I was quite aware of the situation that sometimes when soldiers are coming from the night duties or night patrols, they may be in a different mental state. And when they were seeing us outside, they could show very different reactions. That was my reasoning, and that's why I testified that. Over time, the situation changed, and approximately after one week we were able to go outside. The situation became stable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back to 6622, the previous page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The penultimate sentence in the third passage reads: [In English] "When we stopped, the civilians told me not to worry, that nobody wanted to harm me. When he told me that, I felt better, because I had thought they would shoot us." [Interpretation] Earlier today, on page 20, you stated that you had not been told that your release is conditional upon the end of air-strikes, but rather some sort of the end of hostilities with NATO, that it was conditional on finding a solution to stop hostilities with NATO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I took the words of the journalist. I related them to the situation I found myself in. So what was the situation? I was brought to the high peak, to a place unknown to me, and I didn't know what would happen. So I related that sentence to the situation in which I and Rechner found ourselves, Do not be afraid, nothing will happen to you. So I related that to that very situation. So in this very place, I won't be shot down, definitely. I couldn't think, well, ahead of time. I was only thinking I was happy with what I was experiencing at the given moment and what I knew at the given moment. That's how I recall that. We were blindfolded, and we were not informed where we were going and what we were going there for. So until we reached that place and until that sentence was uttered, I didn't know what was the reason of me going there, and the entire road up the hill was under great stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20, you stated that you were not told that the condition of your release was not the end of air-strikes, but the end of overall hostilities with NATO, or, in other words, finding a solution to that situation between the Republika Srpska and NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible Mr. Karadzic can put the exact words that the witness said to him so that he can see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't find that phrase on page 20.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the witness said. I'm paraphrasing. I'm still trying to find the page. I have some technical problems in accessing the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you stated earlier on, on that page, that you were not told that the condition of your release was not the end of air-strikes, but the end of hostilities, because solutions were being sought to end this conflict or hostilities with NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I agree with you, I can't find anywhere that -- the proposition that Mr. Karadzic is putting to the witness. And he says that he's paraphrasing, but it's simply not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I take it he's trying to find that passage. But in the meantime, Colonel Kalbarczyk, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those who took care of us never spoke about our release. So if I said -- if I quoted the words of that officer on the first day, on the 26th, at 9.00 p.m., who came to us and he said what our situation was, well, the situation depended on the circumstances following on, whether the sides would reach an agreement and the air-strikes would be stopped or not. But that was in no relation to the release, but to the change of the character of our stay in that base. When we were in that base, we all the time were hostages and human shields which they wanted to use in the case of any information that air-strikes were resumed. But nobody said anything about our release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what the witness said on page 20 is this, whether it would help you, but I quote: "He said that our status is not going to change as long as the parties fail to reach an agreement." Is that the passage you refer to? You continued further: "In other words, there must be a clear declaration from the NATO command that they will stop air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have in e-court P2161, please. It was admitted a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, did you know that the United Nations also held some Serbs in custody?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go back to this document later on. For now, could we see P2161, please. Page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 2: [In English] "The Serbian authorities expressed all the time their eagerness of having the four Bosnian Serbs taken hostages by UN released. I told them that the decision of that was dependent on the Special Representative of the Secretary-General decision, but that he was in Geneva ..." And so on. [Interpretation] So you did not know that the UN forces and the Republika Srpska forces actually mutually took prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When I was kind of prisoner of war, we were cut off from any information of that kind. Such documents never reached us. That was impossible. This is a document that was issued on the 14th of June, so after all these events I participated in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I think Mr. Karadzic is misquoting that document. It doesn't say there that the UN mutually -- mutually, the UN and the Republika Srpska forces actually mutually took prisoners. That's not what that document states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. We all can read that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect, that was part of my question. That was whether Mr. Kalbarczyk knew that there was taking of prisoners on the other side as well, and that, as of the 14th of July, they had not been released as yet. Could we now please go back to the previous document, the earlier document, please, and then page 0035-6623. Thank you. Now we have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed for us today that there was a wedding ceremony of some sort there. Would you please look at the last paragraph: [In English] "We left the radar station and stopped in another Olympic building, where a wedding was being celebrated. We were invited to have a drink and eat. Many people came to tell us not to worry. The father of the groom remembered me from my previous patrols and also talked to me. We stayed there for about one and a half hours." [No interpretation]: [In English] "I asked the journalist to call my wife and say that I am okay. Later, I found out that he called my wife and told her I was okay ." [Interpretation] Did you accept this invitation to join this wedding ceremony or celebration?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I did not accept an invitation. That would look strange, given the fact -- given our situation, our enormous stress, simply to allow ourselves to be filmed, us rejoicing in a wedding ceremony. But I do confirm that those people were very friendly to us, and that was very helpful to us. It helped us to detach ourselves from the difficult moments we lived through some time ago when going up the hill, not knowing what for. I'm actually grateful to the journalist. He kept his promise. And my wife later told me that she did not really understand, but Serbian is actually a bit similar to Polish, so she guessed that what he was saying was, Don't worry, everything is okay, your husband is alive, he sends you greetings, and he's going to be back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. Page 624, one before this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, in the central paragraph that begins with the words "Nothing happened during that whole period of time ...": [In English] "On 2nd or 3rd, we were visited by General Mladic, in civilian clothes, and other people in civilian clothes. They wanted to see how we were. At that moment, I did not know it was Mladic, but now that I saw him on TV, I know it was him." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. So you go on to speak about questioning, and you say that your two friends were questioned about the circumstances and whether the UNMOs were actually capable of guiding NATO aircraft and finding the targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I can confirm this. I did not witness this conversation. I'm only telling you what I heard from Evans and the Czech UNMO, Olek, who participated in the conversation. In the witness statement, the word is used "interrogation." It wasn't really an interrogation. I think it might have been just a conversation with the people who visited us. Now, from what I was told, I gathered that the civilians asked -- were asking whether there was any possibility that, with the equipment we had, we could guide and show targets to NATO planes. These were pilots, and that's why they were selected. And also they told me -- my colleagues told me that they had been asked about myself. It was because they knew that I came from the Polish Air Force. However, they explained that I was just a lecturer at a military air academy. Therefore, they decided not to talk to me. This is what my colleagues told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the leader of your team, Griffith Evans from Ghana, was also an air force member -- rather, he was a pilot in his army; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, I said that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Zidlik, Oldrich, also a member of the Czech air forces, in the Czech Army?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I can confirm this on the basis of what they told me. I do not have any documents stating that they were pilots. I did not have any such documents, I did not see any such documents. This is what I -- what they told me and what other colleagues told me, that they were pilots in their home countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if any of the other members of your observation post in Pale, in other words, any other member of your team, was a pilot or a member of the air force?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I do not have any such knowledge. Only these two were mentioned. All others I assume were from other forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at Kasindol, too, and in other places there were pilots who actually served as military observers, so there were both pilots and members of the air forces of different countries?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: This is the first I heard of Kasindol. I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will -- well, rather, let's deal with this page first, and then we will talk about this questioning about guidance of aircraft, and what your colleagues had to say about it. So we'll get back to that later. But for now, would you please take a look at the next paragraph, where you say that Captain Vojvodic took his private car and drove you, on one occasion, to where you were staying, to your accommodations. And I believe at one other place, you also mentioned that on two or three occasions, you actually went to your earlier accommodations, the place where you stayed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: What is exactly said is that we first went to where the Echo 1 team was located, accommodated. We took the remaining personal effects, and on the way back we popped into -- we went to 7 Lima location, where Patrick was, where Olek was. This is where we had satellite connections, and Captain Vojvodic let us use the satellite telephone and make a phone call. This is the first time I could call my wife, and my colleagues, too. I don't remember how many there were; maybe two, maybe one. So where the satellite phone was wasn't my permanent accommodation. It was a different team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, you say that a few days later, you were visited by the ICRC and then also by a doctor. And then you say: [In English] "I asked for some vitamins and I received them the next day. Romero was in bad health condition, and because of the opinion of the doctor, he was the first to be released." [Interpretation] Correct?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Not exactly. What I'm saying is that first we were visited by the Red Cross, and we requested -- after they left, the Red Cross left, one or two days after they left, came the doctor. And the doctor examined everyone, and his decision was that Pepe, the Spaniard, should be in hospital, he's in bad condition, he should be taken away from us as soon as possible. I only asked for vitamins, and I got the vitamins on the next day. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know those two doctors, and you can confirm, right, that one of them was a university professor?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's the title he gave. He was very polite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see or take a look together at this conversation about the guidance of aircraft and what your colleague, Evans, had to say about it. For a moment, I would like to have his statement pulled up in e-court. That's 1D5360 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Exhibit P00051.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it the 65 ter number is 1D3060. Yes, let's pull it up. So this is a statement we admitted pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see page 5 of this document, please. I'm not quite certain that this is page 5. Can we see page 5 of the document, itself, perhaps a page before this one or maybe one after this one. It's a typewritten text, a page of text. Just a moment. As of June 1st --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think that can be found with the ERN at the bottom of the page ending 082.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this paragraph beginning with: "On 1st June 1995 ...": [In English] "... we had a visit from the General Staff, and I was called by a major, leader of the General Staff, for a private interview." [Interpretation] And now he goes on to explain that, basically, they wanted the confirmation of how the NATO got their targets, and they wanted to check whether the rumours that aircraft were guided by UNMOs were correct, and so on and so forth. And then he explains what he told them. Now, do you agree that you, too, did not recognise Mladic at the first blush, as it were, and that your colleague, too, did not recognise -- had not recognised Mladic, that it was a major that he mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't know. I am only telling you here what I felt. Whether they recognised Mladic or not, it's hard for me to say. I had not asked them about this. But I just wanted to say that Evans said it accurately, that it was really even like a private conversation, a discussion, not necessarily an interrogation. They asked about whether there were possibilities that we were, as observers, military observers, able to guide planes and show targets. This is what I know, this is what I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's see what an officer of the Czech Army has to say about this. His name is Oldrich Zidlik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D3061. It may have been admitted already, but I don't know the P number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been admitted, Your Honour. But I would ask that the first page, the cover page, isn't shown because it has the witness's -- may have the witness's contact details on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then we can skip to page 3 right away of that document, paragraph 6. 1D3061, page 3. I don't think this is page 3. Can we see the previous page, please. Just a moment, let me check this. Then it must be an earlier page. So I meant page 3 with the cover page included.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what he says in paragraph 6: [In English] "On the seventh day of our detention, two of us were interrogated by security officers from Lukavica barracks. I was interrogated by an officer who introduced himself as a Major Bukova." I suppose it was Bukva. I know the guy, Bukva. This is not citing. This is not quoting. [Interpretation] This was just my remark. Bukva, that's the name: [In English] "They showed us lists with grids or targets. He said this was information taken from the UNMO computer. I believe it was a fake list. He said that we were guiding NATO aircrafts to the targets. He did not know anything about the subject, not even about basic things of guiding of planes. I was not threatened. He did not refer to the higher military commands." [Interpretation] Can you agree that this colleague of yourself never actually thought that it was Mladic? He, too, didn't think of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It is hard for me to refer to what I have just heard and to what we're reading. It was never discussed in such detail with me. I am surprised by what I read here and hear here, but it is as it is. What I knew only was that the conversation took place. We didn't talk about any details, neither with Olek nor with Evans, so my knowledge in this respect is quite meager. I didn't know that in the computer there were any targets or any data. I was not told this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please take a look at what Gunnar Westlund from Sweden had to say. That's D309, D309. Can we take a brief look at this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, although you hadn't been there for a long time, that there were some military crews in UN vehicles that did not really belong to the UN; in other words, that the vehicles and uniforms of the UN were abused, there were such instances?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I was a fairly young UNMO at that time, and I stayed there for a fairly short time. Therefore, I didn't have such knowledge. I don't have any knowledge of what Gunnar Westlund was saying here. Gunnar told me the same thing when we were at Dubrovnik after the incident in Pale, because we were transferred there together, so I may confirm that he told me that story. Gunnar told me that, but it was when we were transferred to Dubrovnik. He said that he was in such a situation. I never came across anything like that, and I didn't have any information of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think that this is the map you -- that this is the document you referred to. Do you have an exact 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Reid informs me it's D306, not 309, the supplemental information sheet of Gunnar Westlund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the "6" was just misread as "9." So could we have D306, please. Yes, so this is Gunnar Westlund. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 3: [In English] "Once, in April 1995, I looked out our window and I saw a UN vehicle with apparent UNMOs inside it, about 200 metres from our building. UNMOs were always very cautious to notify each other whenever we left our assigned areas and entered another team's area, but no team had contacted us to report a visit to our area." [Interpretation] And then he describes the situation. When they wanted to make contact, the crew left, and then the last sentence says: [In English] "Other UNMOs reported similar incidents." [Interpretation] Do you understand that the Serbian side had to be cautious about the abuse of UN vehicles and insignia, bearing in mind that those vehicles and people could cross the Serb lines and carry out reconnaissance missions, and they were not, as a matter of fact, UN personnel? This is what you heard from Westlund; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Theoretically, it was possible, but I have no knowledge of the practice of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that some Canadian and British troops worked as forward air controllers, and they scouted and guided NATO missiles? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, and I had no interest such things. I was focused on my tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. For planning purposes, can I know how much longer you would need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes or so. I should be able to finish within the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the tape runs only for one and a half -- or one hour and forty minutes, so we need to take a break now. So we'll break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were told that you were under the supervision of the Army of Republika Srpska. Were you kept as prisoners of war? Did anybody mention the term to you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, no one defined our status.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D3059 to see what Harley Alves said about that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Harley Alves was with you, was he not?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: What was his nationality, because Harley -- was it the Brazilian or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was a Brazilian.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: If this is Harley that I mentioned earlier, the Brazilian, I got to know him because he was together with me at the barracks, and I described our relationship earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 in this document. Just a moment, please. Bear with me. It may be page 2. Oh, no, it is here, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, in the last paragraph, he says: [In English] "They brought us some Spanish newspapers, so from that moment we knew that we were considered as prisoners of war by so-called Republika Srpska. After that, we tried to organise ourselves as prisoners of war, and we gave a letter with some requests to Vojvodic. We wanted to be able to contact our families, to watch the news, to have a visit from ICRC and doctors, and we wanted to get in touch with Nikola Koljevic. We also requested to go out to get some shower." [Interpretation] Your colleague was clear that your status was the status of prisoners of war; is that what your colleague says in his statement?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In my statement, I didn't mention that, but there was a situation. I think that it was on the fifth or sixth day. I don't remember clearly. But when we were in the ultimate -- in the final barracks, we decided to write our requests regarding our stay in that place, and there was something like that. We prepared the list of requests, and we actually passed it on to the officer who was in charge. His name was Vojvodic. And I don't quite remember what we put on this list of requests, but I confirm that it happened. And we requested to contact with family and we requested contact with the Red Cross. And perhaps it was after the letter that we prepared, the Red Cross arrived, and then the sanctions were somewhat mitigated and we were able to step outside and we could take a walk in the designated area. So that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D3058. Zlatko Kozusnik, yes, and let's see what he said in his statement. Can we look at page 5 in his statement, page 5. Just a moment, let's see. Four, personally -- second sentence in the fourth paragraph: [In English] "Personally, I would like to say that I felt more safe there than in SE-1 accommodation, because of the local population which was angry with us because of NATO air-strikes." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this remark, with what Zlatko Kozusnik said in his statement?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I may just add that we were just calming our concerns for the practical reasons. We were able to figure out that there was some discussion going on that the situation will be brought to an end, but it didn't change the fact that each of us was aware that if the discussion went in a different direction, then we would come back to the starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that moment, there's no doubt about that, you were an active serviceman and a UN NATO -- a UN member?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I do not quite understand. At what moment? At what moment do you refer? Do you mean my entire mission, when I was a serviceman, or "at the moment" means the day when the trouble began? Please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you were arrested. At that moment, were you an active serviceman and did you serve as a member of the United Nations forces?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When I said that I was a serviceman, my point was that my main task was to take care of the correspondence with headquarters, with Sarajevo, on the radio, and I was responsible for incoming radio correspondence that was reaching our team. So that was my service, while other colleagues could do some other things at that time, perhaps their personal things or some other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And all of them were active servicemen in the United Nations forces; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes, all of them were active servicemen in their respective armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But also in the United Nations forces at the moment when they were arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Of course. The procedure was such that given armed force from the country of origin of the UNMO had to second him to the UN mission, and when the papers were signed, we were reporting to the command of the UN, so the Secretary-General of the United Nations. At that point, my superiors in Poland were no longer relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When talking about the UN observers and others who may have been engaged on some other tasks, do you remember - and you spoke about that on pages 39 and 40 - do you remember a document that was shown to you by Madam Sutherland containing a list of 26 men who had been arrested? Do you remember that only eight of them were UNMOs, whereas the other eighteen captives were not UN observers? Do you remember that document or shall I call it up for you again?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I saw this document yesterday and I also saw it today. I pointed out the names of people that I've known. While I don't know the others, I don't know who they were, this is what I found out, that they were not UNMOs. So this is my knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Colonel. I am sorry that at the moment of our hostility with NATO, you found yourself in the area, but I am also glad that the outcome of all that was good. Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Kalbarczyk, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no further witness for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session. In relation to the third witness scheduled for next week, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber is aware and are appreciative of the efforts being made by the Registry to expedite the process of service of the subpoena on the witness. However, until that service is completed and we have an indication of the witness's reaction to the subpoena -- just a second. Is there a further development?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, I have just read the information. Do you have any follow-up on that? I take it that the Defence is not informed yet. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I presume the Court is looking at the same information that was provided at 1.09. I have not heard anything additional since then. I may be in a position to provide the Court with some clarification of any issues that may arise, because I've been attempting to follow the process as it was underway, so there may be nuances that the Court is concerned about. I don't know what the Court intends to do next. I, frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. But there's no reason not to inform the Defence of this development?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think they've been apprised -- no, I can't think of any reason offhand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll read out what I just received, for your information, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson. This is an e-mail from the Registry to the OTP team, and the main part reads like this: "The witness has informed the VWS that the subpoena was served on him today at 10.33. Mr. Zecevic conveyed to the VWS that as he has written down in the memorandum of service of subpoena, knowing the consequences of the decision, he has decided not to appear before the Court in the Karadzic case in The Hague, nor via videolink, with the primary reason being his negative to appear as the Prosecutor's witness in the case and his poor medical condition as secondary reason." It goes on like this. So we'll consider what the next step should be. But before that, we need to hear from you, Mr. Tieger, what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- are minded to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two matters arise, it seems to me. I would have alerted the Court, in any event -- that is, prior to receiving this, when the matter, as the Court noted, was still even less clear, that we were -- we would be notifying the Court and the Defence about the addition of another witness for next week, in light of the possibility that this third witness would not appear. Obviously, in many respects the information that the Court just read is basically a confirmation of what we knew before, that is, the witness's reluctance to appear voluntarily and the existence of his medical condition. It appears we may have further information from the submission or provision of some medical documentation. So the Prosecution, of course -- the position remains the same. We applied for the subpoena for the reasons stated. They seem to be largely confirmed in the information we've just received. We wish to press forward, but -- as quickly as possible. In that regard, I do note that there was a suggestion by VWS that there would be no processing of the necessary visa application because of the witness's position. I wonder if that really makes sense if the Court wishes to ensure that the subpoena is enforced, so I would note that that issue may arise, and, secondly, that the Prosecution has done and is doing what it can to respond to the, obviously, realistic possibility that this witness will not be present to testify at least on Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that you will make best efforts to make arrangement for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are doing so, and we will continue to do so. I mean, our -- there's only so much we can do. But if the Court was inquiring about our -- I don't think it was. I think it was implicit in our submission of the subpoena in the first place, but, of course, we would continue to maintain the positions taken in our application, and anticipate that the subpoena would be moved on and enforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Legal Officer could approach the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We go back to open session. Do you have any observation before that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Primarily, we're not concerned with the enforcement of the subpoena, but my general suggestion would be that until the time comes when the witness has been ordered to -- has been -- is supposed to appear and he doesn't appear, then the question is premature at this point as to what to do to enforce a subpoena. So next Wednesday, when the case is called, and if he's not here, then I think that would be the time to deal with that issue. But thinking about the scheduling, I can think of very few witnesses who we could be prepared to cross-examine next week, given the notice that we have right now. There is maybe one or two people who give very limited testimony that could possibly be -- we could deal with that on cross-examination. But as we go into the weekend, it really would be impossible to prepare for some witness that we haven't been expecting. So I ask you to consider that when you think about the schedule for next week. If I could also mention, and perhaps this could be in public session, but I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't we go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, thinking about the schedule for next week, I just want to bring to your attention that since the trial resumed on the 13th of January, we have received approximately 18 to 20 disclosure batches, sometimes at a rate of five a day, of Rule 68 and Rule 66(A)(ii) material, and it involves hundreds of documents which have to be examined by our team to determine if they are relevant to the next upcoming witness or to determine whether they should be the subject of disclosure violation motions. Two disclosure violation motions have been filed today. I expect another two to be filed on Monday and probably at least one more after that next week, but we're so far behind in just trying to review the disclosure material that we're receiving at this rate that it's very difficult to keep up with the preparation of cross-examination. So if it turns out that we have one or two days next week in which we don't sit, believe me, we would be putting that time to very good use and it would not be a real waste of time because of these problems we're having with disclosure violations and late disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your submission. The hearing is now adjourned, and we will sit on Monday at 9.00. I'm sorry, 2.30, yes. That's the day when we are sitting 2.30 -- from 2.30 to 6.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of January, 2011, at 2.30 p.m.
